sents: Somewhere on the sea floor, a rock… blinks.
Its skin ripples from sand-grey to coral-red in less than a second.
Then the rock unfolds eight arms, and slips into a gap no wider than a coin.
It has three hearts.
Blue blood.
And most of its brain isn't in its head at all.
It isn't from another planet.
But it might be the closest thing to an alien we will ever meet.
This is the octopus.
To understand how strange that is, go back six hundred million years.
Our last common ancestor with the octopus was probably a tiny, worm-like creature with a very simple nervous system.
From there, our two lineages split.
One road led to fish, reptiles, mammals… and us.
The other led to snails, clams, and oysters.
And then, out of that family of slow, shelled animals, something extraordinary happened.
One branch threw away its shell… and built a mind.
Think about what that means.
Without a shell, an octopus is a soft, boneless, delicious meal.
Its only defence is intelligence.
Its only hard part is a beak, like a parrot's.
So anywhere that beak can fit, the whole animal can follow.
Then there are the hearts.
Two pump blood through the gills.
A third pushes it around the body.
And that blood is blue, because it carries oxygen with copper instead of iron.
But the strangest thing is the brain.
An octopus has around five hundred million neurons… and roughly two thirds of them aren't in its head.
They're in its arms.
Each arm can taste what it touches, through hundreds of suckers.
Each arm can make some of its own decisions.
Researchers have seen a severed arm keep reaching, and grabbing, as if it still had somewhere to be.
Imagine if your fingers could think.
And then, the vanishing act.
An octopus skin is packed with millions of colour cells, each one wired directly to the nervous system.
In a fraction of a second, it can match the colour, the pattern, even the texture of a rock or a reef.
Here's the twist.
Most octopuses are thought to be colour-blind.
Scientists are still debating how they pull this off.
One idea: their skin itself may be able to sense light.
In other words, the octopus might be seeing… with its skin.
Some go even further.
In the waters of Indonesia lives the mimic octopus.
When danger comes, it doesn't just hide.
It becomes something else.
Flattening into a flatfish.
Trailing its arms like the striped spines of a lionfish.
Even posing as a venomous sea snake.
One animal… performing a whole cast of characters.
Their intelligence doesn't stop at disguise.
In 2009, researchers filmed veined octopuses in Indonesia carrying coconut shell halves across the sea floor… then assembling them into a shelter.
It was one of the first cases of an invertebrate carrying tools for later use.
In aquariums, octopuses unscrew jars, recognise individual people, and squirt water at the ones they don't like.
And in 2016, at New Zealand's national aquarium, an octopus named Inky squeezed out of his tank, crossed the floor… and slid down a drainpipe to the open sea.
He was never seen again.
And perhaps strangest of all… octopuses may dream.
When they sleep, their skin usually fades to a calm, pale grey.
But every so often, a sleeping octopus suddenly flashes through a storm of colours.
Its arms twitch.
Its eyes flicker.
Its skin plays out patterns of hunting, and hiding… and then goes still again.
In 2023, scientists reported that octopuses have two stages of sleep, a quiet one, and an active one, with brain activity that echoes waking life.
Nobody knows what, if anything, an octopus experiences in those moments.
But it's hard to watch one and not wonder… what is it seeing?
So, with a mind like that, why haven't octopuses taken over the oceans?
The answer is heartbreaking.
Most octopuses live fast, and die young.
Many species survive only a year or two.
And for a mother, the end is built into the beginning.
She lays her eggs in a den, and guards them.
She cleans them, blows fresh water over them… and stops eating.
Deep off the coast of California, scientists watched one mother guard her eggs for fifty-three months.
Four and a half years, without leaving.
When her young finally hatched… she was gone.
Each new generation starts again from scratch.
No parents.
No teachers.
Everything an octopus knows, it learns alone, in the few short months it has.
And still, it opens jars, builds shelters, and escapes aquariums.
Six hundred million years ago, life on Earth took two roads towards intelligence.
One of them led to us.
The other is still out there, watching from the reef.
And it's watching us right back.
